From: Lincoln HS IT Services <it-support@lincolnhs-helpdesk.com>
Subject: ACTION REQUIRED: Mailbox deactivation in 2 hours

Dear Staff Member,

Our records show your mailbox has not been verified for the new semester. To avoid permanent loss of all email, verify your account within 2 hours using the secure portal below. Most of your colleagues have already completed this step.

cs1d.title: Voicemail left for a district finance clerk, and the district payment policy
cs1d.body:
Voicemail (Friday 4:52 p.m.), in a voice that sounds exactly like Superintendent Ramos:
"Hi Dana, it's Elena. I'm boarding a flight and can't talk. The roofing contractor changed banks, and if they aren't paid by five today we lose the summer slot. Please wire the $48,000 to the new account I'm texting you. Don't loop in the business office, they'll slow it down."

District payment policy, section 4:
• Any change to a vendor's bank details must be confirmed by calling the vendor at the number already on file.
• Payments over $10,000 require approval from two people.
• Staff may not act on payment instructions received only by voicemail, text or chat.

cs5c.title: How a student's browser connects to the school portal
cs5c.body:
1. The portal sends the browser its certificate, which contains the portal's public key and is signed by a trusted certificate authority.
2. The browser checks the signature and the domain name on the certificate.
3. The browser and portal use asymmetric cryptography to agree on a fresh, random session key.
4. For the rest of the visit, every page and form is encrypted with AES using that session key.
5. The portal's private key never leaves the portal's server.

cs5d.title: Code review notes for a new club sign-up app
cs5d.body:
• The 'name' field is checked only in the browser with JavaScript; the server accepts whatever it receives.
• Search builds SQL by joining strings: "SELECT * FROM clubs WHERE name = '" + input + "'".
• Comments are displayed on the page exactly as typed.
• The app's database account has full admin rights on every table.
• A debug page at /debug shows server variables and is enabled in production.
• The app ships with admin login 'admin' / 'admin'.

qs.q: Which TWO social engineering levers are MOST clearly used in the email?
r: Correct. 'Within 2 hours' is urgency, and 'Most of your colleagues have already completed this step' is consensus.
Wrong. It claims to be from IT, but nothing is described as limited in supply.
Wrong. It doesn't pretend to know the teacher personally, and its threat is a deadline, not intimidation by a person.
Wrong. It asks for one action at once rather than drawing out details over time.

qs.q: Which detail in the email is the STRONGEST evidence that it is not really from the school's IT department?
c: The sender and link use the domain lincolnhs-helpdesk.com instead of the school's own domain
The email is addressed to 'Staff Member'
The subject line is in capital letters
r: Correct. A look-alike outside domain for both the sender and the link is hard evidence of impersonation.
Wrong. A generic greeting is a weak signal; real mass emails use them too.
Wrong. Formatting is a weak signal that legitimate senders also use.
Wrong. The signature is just text and is easy to fake.

qs.q: The teacher already clicked the link and entered their password. Which action should come FIRST?
c: Change the password from a trusted device and report the email to IT
Reply to the email to cancel the request
Forward the email to colleagues as a warning
Wait to see whether the mailbox is deactivated
r: Correct. Changing the stolen password quickly and reporting it limits the damage and lets IT protect others.
Wrong. Replying goes to the attacker and doesn't make the stolen password useless.
Wrong. Forwarding spreads the phishing link; IT should send the warning.
Wrong. Waiting gives the attacker time to use the password.

qs.q: What does the sign-in activity show happened at 02:07?
c: An attacker with the correct password got past MFA after repeated push prompts
The student logged in from a trip abroad
The MFA app malfunctioned and approved itself
r: Correct. The password was already right; after a denial and nine more prompts, a push was approved, which is MFA fatigue.
Wrong. Earlier logins put the student in Seattle a few hours before, so this is impossible travel.
Wrong. Push prompts don't approve themselves; a person tapped Approve.
Wrong. The password was correct, and the attack ended in success.

qs.q: Which change would MOST directly have stopped the 02:07 sign-in?
c: Number-matching MFA or a hardware security key instead of simple approve/deny pushes
Requiring the password to be changed every 90 days
r: Correct. These need active, informed input from the user, which defeats blind approvals.
Wrong. Usernames aren't secret and don't stop MFA fatigue.
Wrong. The attacker already had the current password.
Wrong. Alerts help detection; turning them off hides the attack.

qs.q: After the student reports the activity, what should IT do FIRST?
c: Reset the password, end all active sessions, and review the MFA method
Delete the student's account and create a new one next semester
Email the student the new password
r: Correct. Removing the stolen password and the attacker's session contains the compromise.
Wrong. That's drastic, and the attacker's session may remain until it's ended.
Wrong. Seattle is the legitimate location; Lagos is the suspicious one.
Wrong. If the account's email is compromised, the attacker could read it.

qs.q: Which network in the scan is MOST likely an evil twin?
c: The open 'BeanHouse_Guest' from an unknown laptop adapter
The WPA2 'BeanHouse_Guest' on the café's router
r: Correct. It copies the café's network name but runs on unknown hardware with no encryption.
Wrong. This is the café's real network on its own router.
Wrong. This is the café's real staff network.
Wrong. A duplicate name from different, unknown hardware is a classic evil-twin sign.

qs.q: Why might many customers' devices join the open 'BeanHouse_Guest' instead of the real one?
c: Devices often auto-join the strongest signal with a remembered name
r: Correct. The fake has a strong signal and a familiar name, so auto-join picks it.
Wrong. Being open has nothing to do with speed; signal and remembered names drive auto-join.
Wrong. WPA2 works with phones.
Wrong. The real network is broadcasting in the scan.

qs.q: A customer needs to check a bank account. Which plan BEST protects them?
c: Join the WPA2 network after confirming the name with staff, use a VPN, and check the bank's domain before logging in
Join FREE_FAST_WIFI because it has the strongest signal
Join the open BeanHouse_Guest but use private browsing
r: Correct. Verifying the network, encrypting traffic and checking the destination together cover the main risks.
Wrong. An unknown open network may be run by an attacker.
Wrong. One of the two BeanHouse_Guest networks is fake.
Wrong. Private browsing doesn't encrypt traffic or detect a fake access point.

qs.q: The voicemail is MOST likely an example of:
c: AI voice cloning used for payment fraud
r: Correct. A cloned executive's voice requesting an urgent wire transfer is deepfake payment fraud.
Wrong. War driving maps Wi-Fi networks.
Wrong. An evil twin is a fake wireless network.
Wrong. Credential stuffing reuses leaked passwords.

qs.q: Which detail is the STRONGEST red flag, regardless of how real the voice sounds?
c: The request to change bank details and skip the business office conflicts with the payment policy
The voicemail arrives on a Friday
r: Correct. A request that breaks policy and asks to avoid normal checks is suspicious no matter who seems to be asking.
Wrong. Travel is a common, plausible cover story.
Wrong. The amount alone doesn't show fraud.
Wrong. Timing is a weak signal, though attackers do like end-of-week pressure.

qs.q: How does the district's payment policy defend against this attack even if staff cannot tell the voice is fake?
c: It requires out-of-band verification and a second approver, so one convincing call can't move money
It trains staff to hear audio artifacts
r: Correct. Procedural controls work no matter how good the deepfake is.
Wrong. The policy doesn't rely on spotting the fake.
Wrong. Voicemails still arrive; the policy limits what staff do with them.
Wrong. Encryption doesn't verify who made the request.

qs.q: Which risk response is planned for R2?
r: Correct. Insurance shifts the financial impact to a third party.
Wrong. The district isn't stopping the activity; it keeps the data center.
Wrong. Insurance doesn't reduce the chance or the damage of an earthquake.
Wrong. Buying insurance is an action, not acceptance.

qs.q: Which two risks use avoidance and acceptance, in that order?
r: Correct. R3 stops the activity (avoid); R4 deals with it only if it happens (accept).
Wrong. R1 is mitigation and R2 is transfer.
Wrong. R2 is transfer.
Wrong. R4 is acceptance and R1 is mitigation.

qs.q: Which CIA property does R1 MOST directly threaten, and what kind of control are the offline backups?
r: Correct. Encryption by ransomware makes the system unusable, and backups restore it.
Wrong. Ransomware's main harm is lost access, and backups don't prevent the attack.
Wrong. Backups don't detect anything.
Wrong. Backups don't discourage attackers; they recover the data.

qs.q: Which attack is described at 08:10?
r: Correct. The teacher knowingly held the door for someone without a badge.
Wrong. Tailgating happens without the authorized person noticing.
Wrong. No badge data was copied.
Wrong. Nothing was watched.

qs.q: The 11:15 finding MOST directly enables which attack?
r: Correct. Sensitive papers and unwiped drives in the trash are what dumpster divers look for.
Wrong. Pretexting uses a made-up story.
Wrong. Baiting leaves tempting media for victims; here the organization threw its own data out.
Wrong. Elicitation is drawing out information through conversation.

qs.q: The 13:30 caller combines which TWO techniques?
r: Correct. A fake alarm-company role is pretexting, and 'everyone else already gave me the code' is consensus.
Wrong. Nothing is described as limited, and no threat is made.
Wrong. He doesn't claim to know her, and nothing is left as bait.
Wrong. Nothing is observed, and no deadline is set.

qs.q: Which three options give the BEST layered protection against tailgating and after-hours intrusion?
r: Correct. The vestibule prevents tailgating, the camera records who enters, and the motion sensor detects after-hours presence.
Wrong. No preventive control stops tailgating, and a sign isn't a barrier.
Wrong. The sign adds little, and nothing prevents tailgating.
Wrong. Wastes a slot on a sign instead of the camera.

qs.q: Option C is BEST classified as which type and function of control?
r: Correct. It's a physical device that alerts when a door stays open.
Wrong. An alarm doesn't stop someone getting in.
Wrong. It's a device, not a policy.
Wrong. It doesn't restore anything.

qs.q: Why does option A defend against a cloned badge when a badge-only door would not?
c: The PIN is a second factor the attacker doesn't have
r: Correct. A copied card alone won't open the door.
Wrong. Speed isn't the protection.
Wrong. The reader can't tell a good clone from the real card; the PIN is what stops it.
Wrong. PINs don't encrypt badges.

qs.q: Which entry MOST likely shows tailgating or piggybacking?
r: Correct. One granted swipe, a 24-second open door and two people on camera.
Wrong. A normal 5-second entry by one person.
Wrong. The door was never opened; those are denied attempts.
Wrong. One person and a normal open time, though this entry is suspicious for another reason.

qs.q: What does the 02:16 entry MOST likely indicate?
c: M. Ortiz's badge was stolen, cloned or shared
M. Ortiz came in to work overtime
r: Correct. The badge was used while its owner was on leave, at an odd hour.
Wrong. Ortiz is on leave all week.
Wrong. The sensor recorded a normal 6-second open.
Wrong. Nothing suggests an authorized night shift for this badge.

qs.q: At 03:40 the motion sensor triggered with no badge swipe. Which conclusion is BEST supported?
c: Someone was inside without using the reader, either by entering another way or by staying after an earlier entry
The badge reader logged the swipe incorrectly
Motion sensors always trigger at night
It was the 02:16 person leaving normally
r: Correct. Presence without a swipe means the reader was bypassed. The 02:16 entry is a likely lead to investigate.
Wrong. No swipe was attempted at all.
Wrong. A properly tuned sensor in an empty room shouldn't.
Wrong. Leaving wouldn't explain motion inside 84 minutes later, and it still needs investigating.

qs.q: What attack is shown at 09:14?
r: Correct. Forged ARP replies map the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC.
Wrong. Name lookups aren't involved.
Wrong. The switch table isn't being filled with many MACs.
Wrong. There's no ICMP flood.

qs.q: Why does 10.10.0.88 forward traffic onward to the real gateway (09:15:02)?
c: To stay on-path without breaking users' connections, so the attack isn't noticed
r: Correct. Forwarding keeps everything working while the attacker reads the traffic.
Wrong. It adds delay, if anything.
Wrong. Blocking would cause an obvious outage.
Wrong. The attacker isn't encrypting anything.

qs.q: Why is the 09:20:47 event especially HIGH impact?
c: The login was sent over plain HTTP, so the attacker could read the credentials
r: Correct. Unencrypted credentials passing through an on-path attacker can be captured.
Wrong. A POST is a normal way to submit a form.
Wrong. Nothing in the log shows that.
Wrong. Traffic is still being forwarded.

qs.q: Which TWO settings are the MOST serious vulnerabilities?
c: WEP encryption and the default admin password
r: Correct. WEP is broken, and default credentials give anyone admin control.
Wrong. These are weaknesses, but much less severe.
Wrong. Old firmware matters, but a hidden SSID is minor.
Wrong. WPS is serious, but WEP and default admin access are worse.

qs.q: The owner thinks hiding the SSID makes the network secure. Why is that wrong?
c: Hidden SSIDs can be discovered from client traffic, and they don't encrypt anything
r: Correct. Obscurity isn't a control; the real protection comes from encryption and authentication.
Wrong. Speed isn't the issue.
Wrong. Unrelated.
Wrong. Unrelated.

qs.q: Which set of changes BEST hardens this router?
c: WPA3 with AES, WPS off, a unique admin password, updated firmware and lower transmit power
Keep WEP but make the key longer
Broadcast the SSID and keep everything else
r: Correct. Fixes every major weakness in layers.
Wrong. WEP is broken whatever the key length.
Wrong. MAC filtering is easy to bypass and leaves the other flaws.
Wrong. Changes nothing important.

qs.q: Why is the public website in the DMZ rather than the Servers zone?
c: If the website is compromised, firewall rules still separate it from the student records database
The DMZ makes the website load faster
r: Correct. The DMZ contains a breach of internet-facing systems.
Wrong. Speed isn't the purpose.
Wrong. Zones don't encrypt.
Wrong. They could; it would just be riskier.

qs.q: A hallway camera is compromised. Based on the table, what can it reach?
c: The whole internet and all internal zones
r: Correct. The IoT VLAN is allowed to reach only the recorder, which contains the damage.
Wrong. The IoT zone has no path to Servers.
Wrong. There's no path to the Staff VLAN.
Wrong. Its access is limited to the recorder.

qs.q: Which principle does the Guest VLAN rule ('Internet only') apply?
r: Correct. Guests get only the access they need.
Wrong. That splits tasks between people.
Wrong. Nothing is shifted to a third party.
Wrong. Nothing relies on being hidden.

qs.q: A request to TCP 443 arrives from 198.51.100.40. What happens?
r: Correct. Rule 1 matches first, so the deny in Rule 3 is never reached.
Wrong. Rule 3 is never checked for this packet.
Wrong. A rule matched before the implicit deny.
Wrong. Rule 4 is for port 3389.

qs.q: Which rule creates the GREATEST exposure?
c: Rule 2, because it allows SSH from anywhere
Rule 3, because it denies a range
Rule 4, because it allows RDP from 10.0.5.0/24
r: Correct. Remote admin access from the whole internet invites brute-force and exploits.
Wrong. A web server is meant to accept HTTPS.
Wrong. A deny reduces exposure.
Wrong. It's limited to an internal subnet.

qs.q: The team wants 198.51.100.0/24 blocked from everything, and SSH allowed only from 10.0.5.0/24. Which change does BOTH?
c: Move Rule 3 to the top, and change Rule 2's source to 10.0.5.0/24
Add 'Allow TCP 22 from 10.0.5.0/24' at the bottom
r: Correct. The deny now matches first, and SSH is limited to the IT subnet.
Wrong. That blocks HTTPS for everyone and leaves SSH open.
Wrong. That changes nothing about the /24 or SSH.
Wrong. Rule 2 still allows SSH from ANY first.

qs.q: The 07:02 firewall entry is BEST described as:
r: Correct. One source probing many ports in seconds is scanning.
Wrong. It's one source sending a handful of probes.
Wrong. Every attempt was denied.
Wrong. No ICMP flood is involved.

qs.q: Which detection method caught the 07:40 event, and which caught the 08:15 event?
r: Correct. 07:40 matched a known exploit signature; 08:15 deviated from a 50/s baseline.
Wrong. The labels are reversed.
Wrong. 07:40 is explicitly a signature match.
Wrong. 08:15 is explicitly an anomaly.

qs.q: What does the 09:30 entry illustrate?
c: A false negative: an attacker using valid credentials looked normal and wasn't flagged
r: Correct. A real intrusion with no alert is a false negative; behavior that looks normal evades detection.
Wrong. No alert fired, so it can't be a false positive.
Wrong. It wasn't detected at the time.
Wrong. It was a VPN login.

qs.q: Based on 10:02-10:05, the downloaded program is BEST classified as a:
r: Correct. It was disguised as a useful tool and then opened a channel for remote commands.
Wrong. It was installed by a user, though it later spreads.
Wrong. No trigger condition is described.
Wrong. It does far more than show ads.

qs.q: What capability does the Thursday 14:20 entry show?
r: Correct. Recording keystrokes to a file is keylogging.
Wrong. Nothing was encrypted.
Wrong. This entry is about capturing typing, not hiding.
Wrong. No service was disrupted.

qs.q: The Friday 09:00 entry represents which attack phase?
r: Correct. Spreading from one PC to others inside the network.
Wrong. Reconnaissance comes before the attack.
Wrong. Initial access was on Monday.
Wrong. Copying itself is spreading, not sending data out.

qs.q: What can an attacker conclude about abaker and cdiaz from the leaked table?
c: They use the same password, because their unsalted hashes are identical
Their passwords are long and unique
r: Correct. Without salt, identical passwords produce identical hashes.
Wrong. Usernames are plain text.
Wrong. The policy says no MFA.
Wrong. Identical hashes for common passwords suggest the opposite.

qs.q: Why are the hashes for abaker and bchen likely to be cracked almost instantly?
c: Unsalted MD5 hashes of common passwords appear in precomputed rainbow tables
MD5 hashes can be decrypted with a key
r: Correct. Lookups in precomputed tables reverse common unsalted hashes.
Wrong. Hashes have no decryption key.
Wrong. Sorting doesn't matter.
Wrong. Username length doesn't matter.

qs.q: Which set of changes BEST fixes the problems shown?
c: Use a modern salted hash, require at least 14 characters, enable lockout and MFA
Switch to SHA-1 and keep the other settings
r: Correct. Salted strong hashing protects stored passwords, while length, lockout and MFA protect logins.
Wrong. SHA-1 is deprecated, and nothing else improves.
Wrong. The data has already leaked.
Wrong. Frequent changes don't fix weak storage or the lack of MFA.

qs.q: Which laptop is at the HIGHEST risk, and why?
c: T-02: unpatched critical flaws, firewall off and admin rights
r: Correct. Known exploitable flaws, no host filtering and full privileges together.
Wrong. T-01 is well protected.
Wrong. T-03 has issues, but fewer than T-02.
Wrong. T-02 combines the most weaknesses.

qs.q: Which change fixes T-03's firewall problem?
c: Change the inbound RDP rule to deny, or limit it to the IT subnet
r: Correct. RDP shouldn't be open to everyone.
Wrong. That doesn't address inbound RDP.
Wrong. That removes all filtering.
Wrong. That adds exposure.

qs.q: Why is T-03's anti-malware a concern even though the laptop is otherwise patched?
c: Eight-month-old signatures won't recognize newer malware
r: Correct. Signature detection depends on current definitions.
Wrong. Performance isn't the concern.
Wrong. False.
Wrong. Patching and anti-malware cover different risks.

qs.q: Which attacks are shown in Cases 1 and 2, in order?
r: Correct. Case 1 makes 312 tries on one account; Case 2 makes one try each on 1,200 accounts.
Wrong. Reversed.
Wrong. Case 1 targets a single account repeatedly.
Wrong. Case 2's pattern of one try per account from one source fits spraying with a common password.

qs.q: Why didn't lockout stop the success for nwong in Case 2?
c: Spraying made only one attempt per account, staying under the lockout threshold
r: Correct. Spraying is designed to avoid per-account lockout.
Wrong. Nothing in the log suggests that.
Wrong. The attacker had no MFA factor.
Wrong. Case 1 shows lockout applying, and nothing suggests it's limited to admins.

qs.q: Case 3 is BEST explained by:
c: Stolen credentials used directly (for example from phishing or reuse), followed by data exfiltration
r: Correct. A clean login at 3 a.m. from abroad, then a bulk download.
Wrong. There were no failures.
Wrong. Only one account is involved, with no failures.
Wrong. The time, the location and the 180-file download aren't normal.

qs.q: Which attack succeeds at 10:03?
r: Correct. Input changed the query so it returned every row.
